Introduction The contribution of capital markets to economic growth and development cannot be overemphasised. The markets function as central financial institutions which unite investors and fund seekers through domestic and international investment platforms (Algaeed, 2021). The capital market is essential in emerging economies because it supports financing long-term infrastructure projects and manufacturing investments that drive economic development (Megersa, 2020). Saudi Arabia values its capital market because it is a crucial mechanism to facilitate economic development through diversification. The Vision 2030 strategy has made it imperative for Saudi Arabia to decrease its oil export dependency while encouraging investments in non-oil business sectors (Guendouz and Ouassaf, 2020). Ho and Njindan Iyke (2017) have also failed to capture intricacies of the macroeconomic conditions towards stock market performance in developing economies and at the same time acknowledging the critical importance of stock markets in economic development. Saudi Arabian policymakers, financial analysts, and investors must gain a complete understanding of the stock market performance determinants since they influence the economic sustainability and stability of the market (Omri et al., 2019). The role of stock markets has become increasingly important in the context of economic growth (Lusardi, 2019). However, the influence of various macroeconomic forces on stock market performance remains unclear and under-researched, particularly in developing economies and the literature concerning emerging markets. Most studies focus on only a few macroeconomic variables, often neglecting the broader range of factors that affect stock market patterns. This study bridges the gap through an all-round analysis of macroeconomic determinants affecting Saudi Arabia's stock market for thirty years spanning 1991 to 2021. Economic development is closely related to the growth and efficiency of financial markets, where stock markets provide a crucial ground for capital allocation (Shahbaz et al., 2022). Stock markets bridge the gap between capital suppliers and firms that require investment. Therefore, the efficiency of such markets improves economic efficiency and financial stability, resulting in better investment opportunities. This study's results will contribute in various ways to the existing literature. This research makes a significant contribution by offering a comprehensive and long-term investigation into the Saudi stock market’s behaviour using a broader set of macroeconomic indicators than prior studies. While previous literature tends to be fragmented or limited in scope, this study enhances academic understanding by evaluating the dynamic impact of multiple macroeconomic variables—including GDP, inflation, FDI, government expenditure, and trade balance—on stock market performance. By adopting robust econometric methods, the research provides nuanced insights into both short-run adjustments and long-term equilibrium trends, contributing original empirical evidence to the scarce literature on emerging stock markets. Additionally, the analysis of causal relationships and dynamic interactions aids in formulating informed macroeconomic policies to promote market stability and investment opportunities. Most studies have shown correlations between economic indicators and stock market performance. One of the most significant issues with past studies is that they only employed a limited number of economic indicators when researching the stock market in Saudi Arabia. This research seeks to rectify this by using various economic indicators to determine how they affect stock market fluctuations. In doing so, the study offers both theoretical value and practical policy recommendations, enhancing the understanding of macro-financial linkages in Saudi Arabia's context. To achieve this aim, the research project will address the following fundamental questions: − What is the relationship between key macroeconomic variables and the performance of the Saudi stock market? − Do the identified macroeconomic variables exhibit short-run and long-run equilibrium relationships with the Saudi stock market? − Which macroeconomic variable has the most significant causal relationship with Saudi stock market performance? − How closely do changes in the Saudi stock market relate to changes in the chosen macroeconomic variables? The study employs advanced econometric techniques to explore these relationships systematically, namely the Johansen cointegration test and the vector error correction model (VECM) (Elneel & AlMulhim, 2022). These allow for an exhaustive examination of short-run and long-run connections between macroeconomic variables and stock market behaviour, providing a good understanding of the stability and sensitivity of the Saudi stock market to economic shocks. The paper is structured in the following order: Section 2 covers the main literature, Section 3 describes the methodology and data sources, Section 4 covers the results, Section 5 covers the discussion, and Section 6 concludes with policy implications. 2. Literature Review 2.1 Macroeconomic Indicators and Stock Market Performance Extensive research has been conducted on the relationship between macroeconomic indicators and stock market performance. Multiple researchers have examined how various economic factors influence stock market prices. During the early stages of research, scholars examined how GDP growth, unemployment statistics, and inflation affected stock market trends. GDP growth creates a positive link with stock price values because economic expansion enhances investor sentiment, leading to higher stock valuations (Ho and Njindan Iyke, 2017). The research conducted by Amor and Hassine (2017) established that enhancing unemployment rates negatively influenced stock market performance. Stock prices tend to decrease during economic recessions, while labour market instability is another determinant for falling stock market valuations. The factors determining stock market performance due to inflation are difficult to understand. Inflation levels between zero and five per cent benefit stock prices because they drive economic expansion, according to Zhang (2021). Reasons for fast-rising inflation tend to dissolve investor confidence, which weakens market consistency (Filipović, 2024). Researchers have studied these relations in various economic settings using multiple empirical investigations. Queku et al. (2022) examined stock market impacts from macroeconomic indicators using quarterly data for the Ghana Stock Exchange spanning 1991-2005. A previous study by Kyereboah-Coleman and Agyire-Tettey (2008) utilized the Ghana Stock Exchange M.S. B. Elsharif and S. I. M. Hassan / Decision Science Letters 15 (2026) 25 as a case study to study the nexus between macroeconomic variables and stock market performance. In their research, Queku et al. (2022) adopted cointegration methods alongside an error correction model to demonstrate that elevated deposit money bank lending rates restricted stock market performance, thus limiting business growth potential. Their analysis demonstrated a negative correlation between stock market performance and inflation, which confirms the risk that rising prices create for investment returns. 2.2 Global Studies on Macroeconomic Influences There is evidence which shows that the research on economic indicators and on stock prices has been rapidly advancing in the last decades. Interest rates, foreign trade and inflation, stock indices, and economic growth were found by Raza et al. (2023) to be the key short-term HPI determinants of Spain. The study demonstrated the interconnectedness of market shifts that happen in specific main economic variables through the different sorts of asset classes in stock markets. In Malaysia, Mohd Idris (2023) focused on examining the relation between money supply and interest rate and its effectiveness in explaining volatilities of both the stock and real estate markets. From the analysis it was concluded that the equity market and real estate improved when income rose and when Monetary policy moved in an expansionary manner. There was a negative correlation between interest rate and real estate price while stock market has direct correlation with GDP per capita and CPI. Rapaeye (2017) considers the long-standing equilibrium relationships between stock prices of Botswana for which they used data from the period 1998 to 2012 in their quarterly data set. Their examination was based mainly on cointegration analysis. The panel combines various macroeconomic factors, such as GDP and several control variables, including interest rates, money supply, the level of foreign reserves, inflation, exchange rates, diamond price index, and US government bond yields. These variables also showed a positive relationship with stock prices with real GDP, short-term interest rate and the price index and inflation rates. On the other hand, the long-term interest rate, money supply, foreign reserves and exchange rates negatively affected the stock prices. The case highlights the complexity of stock market interactions, where indicators have direct and negative correlation. 2.3 Macroeconomic Determinants of Stock Market in Emerging Economies Alsalloum (2023) extended the analysis of the connection between stock prices and economic indicators by pointing out that, after all, macroeconomic fundamentals are the foundation for any evaluation in the market. This has highlighted the following indicators that could be used to understand the overall behaviour of the stock market at one point in time since the various factors under consideration are not independent and impact investor perception and the price value of securities. Omodero and Mlanga (2019) investigated the impact of macroeconomic variables on the Nigerian stock market using annual time series data from 2009 to 2018. The regression analysis of Omodero and Mlanga revealed that, although the exchange rate and interest rates did not have any statistically significant influence on the stock market index, inflation had a negative significant influence. These findings indicate that inflationary pressures in Nigeria undermine investor confidence and erode real investment returns, making the emerging stock markets sensitive to price stability. Further, these works serve as useful contributions when it comes to obtaining insight on the correlation of macroeconomic variables to stock market performance but most encompass either short-term fluctuations or a small range of macroeconomic variables. Finding studies that address the long-run approach in the development of the stock market in the Saudi Arabian context with a sophisticated methodology like the cointegrations analysis with error correction modelling is relatively rare. The Saudi Arabia economy contains certain peculiarities concerning their dependence on oil, fluctuations in fiscal policies, and persevering reform agenda to diversify their economy (Alzubair, 2021). 3. Methodology and Data Description 3.1 Model Specification This work aims to investigate stock market-performance relations among variables developed in economic theory and verified by empirical evidence. The five macroeconomic indicators that will be chosen initially are Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth rates, inflation (INF), Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), trade openness (TR), and government expenditure (GE). Nevertheless, interest rate (IR) has also been included in the model according to recent studies demonstrating how the dynamic nature of monetary policy impacts capital markets. Interest rates influence investing, cost of borrowing funds, and capital flows and therefore it is a critical factor in the determination of stock market behaviour in emerging and developed economies. These macroeconomic variables are chosen not only on theoretical considerations but also on empirical research that uniformly points to the role that they play on market performance in capital markets. GDP indicates total economic activity; inflation signifies price stability; FDI indicates international investor confidence; trade openness indicates global integration and government expenditure indicates fiscal policy and investment. The final empirical model thereby comprises 6 main explanatory variables: GDP, INF, FDI, TR, GE and IR. The dependent variable is still market capitalization (SM) to measure the performance of the stock market as measuring the total value of listed domestic companies. The study evaluates both the past and the present performance of stock markets in Saudi Arabia using time series econometric analysis of macroeconomic effects. The study focuses on the entire causality relationship between these macro-economic factors in both the long-run and short-run period. As evidenced in numerous research studies, such as Al Rasasi et al. (2019), the macroeconomic fundamentals 26 influence the functioning of capital markets. The research employs the Vector Error Correction Model to test the functional character of the performance on the stock market indices over macroeconomic indices. Despite the relevance in determining the economic activity and market stability of the focus of the theoretical model and data description, Government Expenditure (GE) was not used in the final Vector Error Correction Model estimation, though it was initially applied in the theoretical model and data description. This was decided by the multicollinearity diagnostics and initial statistical tests and results which showed strong correlation between GE and the other explanatory variables GDP and trade openness. The addition of GE rendered the model unstable, and overstated standard errors. Thus, GE was not included in the final estimation to be robust and to have parsimony of models. The exclusion suggests that though fiscal spending can affect the stock market indirectly, its impact can be already accommodated in the GDP and other macroeconomics channels. The Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) uses Johansen's (1991;1995), cointegration approach to detect misspecification biases, while traditional Vector Autoregressive (VAR) models do not have this ability (Balsalobre-Lorente et al., 2019). Standard VAR models demonstrate inadequacy when studying data with sharp long-term variable connections because they are unable to separate short-term effects from equilibrium period relationships. This econometric tool effectively addresses both short-term and long-term dynamics through its combination of features so it proves to be a better analysis method. The choice of VECM is justified because it allows for assessing the dynamic relationships among variables that are non-stationary but cointegrated, which is commonly the case in macroeconomic time series. Unlike static models, VECM provides short-run adjustments and long-run equilibrium relationships, making it suitable for policy analysis. The sample period of 1991 to 2021 was chosen due to the availability of consistent and reliable macroeconomic data from both the World Bank and the Central Bank of Saudi Arabia. It captures important structural economic developments in Saudi Arabia, including economic diversification efforts, trade liberalisation, and public financial reforms under Vision 2030. B. Elsharif and S. I. M. Hassan / Decision Science Letters 15 (2026) 27 The ECM term of VECM supports to interpret the fluctuations in the system economically. The λ coefficient depicts how rapidly the returns of the stock market approach the equilibrium given a shock according to Garlappi and Song (2017). When the value of λ is negative, this relationship is statistically significant, which means that variables have a balance relation over time since anomalies in the stock market are expected to normalise in the future (Singh & Kishor, 2017). The 0.5 value of λ shows that the stock market reduces half the magnitude of its disequilibrium in each period. The reaction pattern of the stock market to economic shocks becomes crucial information for policymakers and investors to know. 3.2 Data Description The data employed in the study is obtained from the World Bank and the Central Bank of Saudi Arabia. It covers a 31-year period (1991–2021), offering a sufficiently long historical context to capture the impacts of cyclical economic movements and structural economic policy changes in Saudi Arabia. This range was selected to ensure data completeness and reduce sample bias. The macroeconomic determinants selected are well-documented in the literature as significant factors influencing stock market performance. The dependent variable of this study is the performance of the stock market, measured by market capitalisation. Market capitalisation is the total value of listed companies and is considered to be a broad measure of the activity and investor confidence in the stock market (Smales, 2017). The independent variables are as follows: − Gross Domestic Product (GDP): This variable is represented by the annual growth rate (%). It measures overall economic growth and is expected to have a positive relationship with the stock market performance (Algaeed, 2021). − Inflation (INF): This is measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which indicates price stability and purchasing power. High inflation is believed to reduce stock market returns, while moderate inflation is seen as beneficial (Fakieh, 2018). − Foreign Direct Investment (FDI): FDI, as a percentage of GDP, is foreign capital inflow into the economy. This increases the liquidity of markets and economic growth (Algarini, 2020). − Trade Openness (TR): This variable, expresses trade as (exports + imports)/GDP, capturing international integration of the global economy and its effects on stock market performance (Mohammed, 2024). − Government Expenditure (GE): Government spending is taken in constant U.S. dollars and affects growth, infrastructure development, and market stability (Binzaid, 2019). − Interest Rate (IR): Interest rate reflects the cost of capital and is typically associated with monetary policy stance. It influences investor behaviour, consumption, and capital investment decisions. In this study, the interest rate is included as a key macroeconomic factor and is expected to have a mixed effect—potentially supporting investment at lower levels while reducing liquidity and equity investment at higher levels (Fakieh, 2018). Results 4.1 Stationary Test It will be crucial to determine whether the data series are stationary, and hence their reliability and accuracies in statistical analysis. A stationary series has its mean, variance, and autocovariance constant over time, thereby being suitable for time- series modelling. Thus, this research submitted the variables under study to an Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test administered by Dickey and Fuller in 1979 and 1981. The test was done both in level form and first-difference form to determine whether the variables are I(0) or higher orders, such as I(1). The results presented in Table 2 reveal that all the tested variables are non-stationary at their levels, which suggests that their statistical properties have evolved over time. When analyzing the first difference of all of these variables, all of the variables were found to be also integrated of the same order, namely, I(1). This assumption is vital, particularly when using variables in econometrics, as failure to test for nonstationarity results in possible spurious regression and invalid relationships between the variables used. The common tendencies can exist instead of genuine connection in the sphere of economics. From the methodological point of view, it depends on the stationarity of the variables. When the variables are at different levels, however, the appropriate approach would be the VAR model if the variables are stationary. However, given that all the variables are stationary at first difference and have the same order of integration, then the VECM is suitable. The Johansen cointegration test will be used to determine whether the variables move together over time (Jalil & Rao, 2019). Cointegration indicates that while the variables may experience short-term fluctuations, they maintain a stable long-term relationship. Any deviation from this equilibrium is expected to be corrected in the long run. In terms of error correction mechanism, it is defined as the speed at which disequilibrium in the system persists during subsequent periods. In this study, the coefficient of ECM was -0.859, which shows that about 85.9% of any disequilibrium is corrected in subsequent periods. The implication is that the adjustment process is relatively quick, whereby departures from the long-run equilibrium are quickly diminished with time. The stock market index (SM) shows positive autocorrelation, with its second lag (L2D.SM) having a significant 30 coefficient of (0.82, p = 0.01), indicating momentum in price adjustments. GDP exhibits a short-run positive effect on stock performance, with the second lag (L2D.GDP) being significant at the 5% level (0.34, p = 0.05), suggesting that economic growth increases investor confidence in the near term. Inflation (INF) has a mixed influence: the first lag (LD.INF) shows a significant positive effect (0.28, p = 0.04), indicating that moderate inflation may stimulate equity investment. However, its influence diminishes in subsequent periods, consistent with inflation volatility affecting purchasing power. Interest rate (IR) changes at the first lag also significantly boost market performance (0.34, p = 0.04), but this effect tapers off, implying a temporary incentive for stock investment under lower interest conditions. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) exerts a negative influence in the short term. The second lag (L2D.FDI) is significant and negative (-0.36, p = 0.04), which may reflect inefficient capital allocation or capital flight risks. Trade openness (TR) displays a significant positive impact at its second lag (0.08, p = 0.00), indicating that increased trade activities enhance market confidence and liquidity in the short term. Long-Run Dynamics The long-run results provide insights into the equilibrium relationship between macroeconomic fundamentals and the Saudi stock market. GDP has a positive coefficient (0.40), though not statistically significant, implying that sustained economic growth generally enhances market capitalisation. Inflation has a negative long-run coefficient (-0.19), indicating that persistent inflation erodes real investment returns and suppresses stock prices over time, though this result is not significant. Interest rate (IR) shows a statistically significant and strong positive effect (0.45, p = 0.00), suggesting that over time, higher interest rates might reflect improved economic activity or attract portfolio investments into stocks. Conversely, FDI carries a large and significant negative coefficient (-0.87, p = 0.00), indicating that in the Saudi context, foreign capital inflows may displace local investment or fail to translate into productive market activity. Trade openness (TR) has a small positive and marginally significant coefficient (0.03, p = 0.09), suggesting that long-term trade liberalisation supports gradual market development. Overall, the long-run equation confirms that structural macroeconomic fundamentals, particularly FDI and IR, play a vital role in shaping stock market behaviour in Saudi Arabia. 4.4 Post-Estimation Diagnostic Tests The post-estimation diagnostic tests evaluate the model's adequacy and reliability at estimating the vector error correction. Three key tests were conducted for this purpose. These include Lagrange Multiplier (LM), Jarque-Bera, and the root of the companion matrix tests. As such, tests were conducted concerning serial correlation LM test to check for its presence in residual series, which may also mean inefficient estimates. The Jarque-Bera test checks whether the residuals are normally distributed; this is a prerequisite for valid statistical inferences. The stability test checks whether all the roots of the companion matrix fall inside the unit circle, meaning the model does not have explosive behaviour and is also appropriate for forecasting. Fluctuations around zero indicate that while deviations may occur in the short run, the variables return to equilibrium. Significant deviations during the late 1990s, early 2000s, and post-2020 periods probably result from economic shocks such as financial crises and the COVID-19 pandemic. Sharp increases post-2020 suggest that the correction mechanism is strong and possibly driven by economic recovery policies. M.S. B. Elsharif and S. I. M. The occurrence of autocorrelation means that the model might be misspecified, thereby making the estimates of parameters inefficient. Table 7 shows the LM test result. Chi-square values for lags 1 and 2 are 31.2606 and 33.2665, respectively, while the respective p-values are 0.69342 and 0.59929. Since these p-values are greater than the conventional significance levels (e.g., 0.05 or 0.01), the null hypothesis of no autocorrelation at the given lag orders cannot be rejected. This suggests that the model's residuals are not serially correlated, meaning that the model is correctly specified in capturing the underlying data dynamics. Discussion The research findings show that macroeconomic variables, particularly GDP growth, inflation, and FDI and trade balance alongside government expenditure, affect Saudi Arabian stock market performance. The cointegration tests validate the existence of long-term equilibrium connections in line with Shahbaz et al. (2022) who proved financial markets depend on economic growth. According to Ho and Njindan Iyke (2017), economic growth leads to increased investor confidence and capital market benefits, as confirmed by the findings between GDP and stock market performance. Research by Filipović (2024) supports the finding that stock returns decrease when inflation rises due to the erosion of real investment values and overall market volatility. The short-term negative effects of FDI run counter to standard market stabilisation perspectives that typically consider foreign investments as stabilising elements. The study shows this unexpected result stems from both capital flight risks and inefficient foreign fund allocation according to Omodero and Mlanga (2019). The research confirms that trade openness is a vital factor supporting market stability, exactly like Mohammed (2024) found globalisation to strengthen market resilience. According to the vector error correction model, the Saudi stock market exhibits quick deviation adjustment, showing its dynamic characteristics. The study demonstrates that policymakers should focus on maintaining economic stability through proper strategies to manage inflation risks to improve stock market performance. 6. Conclusion In this study, all variables that affect the Saudi stock market performance were examined, including GDP growth, inflation, FDI, trade balance, and government expenditure. The paper provides evidence that these economic factors work on stock prices on both short and long run periods, underlining the significance of a stable economy for the stock market. Vector Error Correction Model results show that the Saudi stock market is responsive to the existing economic changes in the environment which maintains balance for a long time. The growth of the stock market has to happen in a steady macro economy for the achievement of the goals leading to its effective operation. On the positive note, financial growth leads to a favourable investment climate but inflation control and imbalance in FDI distribution disrupt market dynamics. Different policy implications contribute to the economic stability of a particular market holding open trade along with government expenditure escalating the necessity of correct economic vulnerability policies. Thus, the research demonstrates the following propositions that have relevance to the study of scholarly researchers, policy specialists and the financial market. Saudi Arabia will implement long term economic sustainable development by enhancing the performance of the financial market while also increasing economic stability for the purpose of increasing stock market stability as well as diversifying the economy. Collected data supports the set of proposed policies guidelines. Thus, the Saudi government has to carry out stabilised macroeconomic policies by means of monetary policies to regulate inflation rates for the further development of the country’s economy. Policymakers should maintain a good price stability to positively impact investments since a fluctuating inflation index hurts the stock market. It is essential for the Saudi government to have policies emerging on economic development other than a speculative manner to make effective FDI in the country. JSON: Name: saudi_macroecon_vecm Title: Johansen cointegration and vector error correction analysis of macroeconomic determinants of Saudi stock market capitalization Short Hypothesis: Over the period 1991–2021 in Saudi Arabia, GDP growth and trade openness causally increase stock market capitalization in the long run while higher inflation and FDI causally decrease stock market capitalization, as detectable by Johansen cointegration and VECM estimation. Related Work: Existing empirical approaches to macroeconomic determinants of stock markets include single-equation regressions, VAR/ARDL frameworks, and cointegration-based estimators (e.g., FMOLS/DOLS). Limitations of prior work are: (1) many studies use restricted variable sets (e.g., only GDP and inflation), producing omitted-variable bias; (2) short samples or quarterly windows that miss structural regime shifts in emerging markets; (3) reliance on VAR or OLS in levels that do not separate short-run dynamics from long-run equilibrium or that ignore cointegration, yielding biased inference when series are I(1); (4) inconsistent treatment of endogeneity and reverse causality between macro variables and market outcomes; (5) limited robustness checks for multicollinearity (e.g., government expenditure vs GDP), structural breaks, and alternative estimators. These weaknesses leave unresolved which macro factors have stable long-run effects, their short-run adjustment speeds, and the robustness of signs and magnitudes across estimation methods. Abstract: This study examines the long-run and short-run causal effects of macroeconomic variables on Saudi stock market capitalization using Johansen cointegration and a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) for 1991–2021. The problem addressed is identifying which macro fundamentals—GDP growth, inflation, foreign direct investment, trade openness, and interest rate—form a stable long-run equilibrium with market capitalization and how shocks are transmitted in the short run. At a high level, the approach applies unit-root testing, Johansen trace and eigenvalue cointegration tests, lag selection by information criteria, VECM estimation with normalized long-run coefficients, and impulse-response and forecast-error variance decomposition analyses. The main contribution is a comprehensive, multivariate identification of both equilibrium relationships and adjustment dynamics in a commodity-exporting emerging market using multiple robustness comparisons (VAR, ARDL, FMOLS/DOLS) and ablations (excluding collinear fiscal variables). Expected outcomes are a small number of cointegrating relations, estimated long-run signs and magnitudes for each macro factor, and an empirically measured speed of correction of disequilibria, informing macro-financial policy design. Experiments: Datasets: annual series 1991–2021 from World Bank and Saudi Central Bank for market capitalization (constant US$), GDP annual growth (%), CPI inflation (%), FDI (% of GDP), trade openness ((exports+imports)/GDP %), interest rate (policy or lending %), government expenditure (constant US$). Preprocessing: natural logs for level variables where applicable; compute first differences; handle missing values by interpolation only if <2 consecutive years. Baselines: (A) OLS-level regression on log market cap, (B) VAR in differences, (C) ARDL bounds test and ECM, (D) FMOLS and DOLS cointegration estimators. Primary method: Johansen cointegration (trace and max-eigen tests) followed by VECM with lag selected by AIC/SIC/HQIC. Evaluation metrics: cointegration rank (trace/eigenvalue p-values), long-run coefficient estimates and t-stats, ECM coefficient (speed of adjustment) and significance, impulse response functions with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, forecast RMSE and MAE on 5-year rolling holdout, Diebold-Mariano test for forecast comparisons, Granger causality p-values, and forecast-error variance decomposition proportions. Experimental setup: (1) unit-root tests (ADF/PP) to confirm I(1); (2) select deterministic trend for Johansen; (3) estimate cointegration rank; (4) estimate VECM and compute IRFs and FEVD with 1000 bootstrap replications; (5) out-of-sample forecast evaluation using last 5 years as holdout; (6) ablation studies: (i) run VECM including government expenditure vs excluding it (test multicollinearity effects), (ii) remove FDI to observe coefficient stability, (iii) replace market capitalization with annual market return as dependent variable; (7) robustness comparisons: VECM vs ARDL vs FMOLS/DOLS vs VAR using identical samples and lag selection criteria. Report statistical significance, coefficient signs, forecast errors, and stability diagnostics for each experiment. Risk Factors and Limitations: Small sample size (31 annual observations) reduces power, increases estimator variance, and limits the number of lags and covariates that can be reliably estimated. Structural breaks (e.g., oil shocks, 2008 crisis, COVID-19, Vision 2030 reforms) can invalidate unit-root and cointegration assumptions and bias long-run estimates. Multicollinearity (notably government expenditure with GDP and trade openness) can inflate standard errors and obscure individual coefficient interpretation. Endogeneity and reverse causality between stock market and macro variables (e.g., capital flows reacting to market conditions) may bias estimates; VECM accounts for dynamics but may not fully resolve contemporaneous endogeneity. Measurement error in FDI and market capitalization data and changes in reporting methodology can distort results. Residual non-normality and heteroskedasticity (observed in FDI residuals) reduce validity of standard inference; bootstrap helps but is computationally intensive. Annual frequency limits detection of high-frequency dynamics and short-lived shocks. External validity is constrained: findings for Saudi Arabia (1991–2021) may not generalize to other countries or to post-2021 regimes.
